entry.title: Ms Erica Bosloper v Linkpoint Lawyers Pty Ltd & Mr Jun Pan [2026] FWC 4208
entry.content:
In [2026] FWC 4208, the Fair Work Commission considered a jurisdictional objection by Linkpoint Lawyers Pty Ltd and Jun Pan to Erica Bosloper’s s 365 application, contending she was not an employee and therefore could not have been dismissed. The Commission examined the written “Partnership Agreement” and how it was performed in practice, and found she was an employee dismissed on the employer’s initiative. The objection was dismissed.

Key holding: Under s 15AA, whether a person is an employee is determined by the real substance, practical reality and true nature of the relationship, considering the totality including actual performance, and is not controlled by the parties’ expressed intention or contractual label.

But the analysis required by section 15AA is not confined to the parties' intentions, or to the terms by which they recorded their intentions. This is made clear in the section itself, as confirmed in the authorities to which I have referred.

entry.title: Application by Colac Otway Disability Accommodation Incorporated [2026] FWC 4213
entry.content:
CODA applied under s 244 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) to be removed from a supported bargaining authorisation covering disability services employers. The Fair Work Commission was satisfied that changed operational, organisational and funding circumstances meant CODA should no longer be specified, and granted the variation.

Key holding: Under s 244(2) of the FW Act, the Commission must vary a supported bargaining authorisation to remove an employer where a change in the employer’s circumstances means it is no longer appropriate for that employer to remain specified.

If an application is made under subsection (1), the FWC must vary the authorisation to remove the employer's name if the FWC is satisfied that, because of a change in the employer's circumstances, it is no longer appropriate for the employer to be specified in the authorisation.

entry.title: Mrs Kristie Maggar v Laura Brown [2026] FWC 4197
entry.content:
LN Veterinary sought costs after Ms Maggar discontinued her unfair dismissal application. The Fair Work Commission refused costs under s 611(2), but ordered $980.75 under s 400A for unreasonable procedural conduct concerning a late adjournment request and failure to instruct her lawyer. The decision is [2026] FWC 4197 (Commissioner McKinnon, 28 October 2026).

Key holding: Under s 400A, costs may be ordered where a party’s unreasonable act or omission in connection with the conduct or continuation of the matter caused the other party to incur costs.

The FWC may make an order for costs against a party to a matter arising under this Part (the first party) for costs incurred by the other party to the matter if the FWC is satisfied that the first party caused those costs to be incurred because of an unreasonable act or omission of the first party in connection with the conduct or continuation of the matter.

entry.title: Danielle Leonard v Cadence Talent Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4161
entry.content:
Danielle Leonard lodged a s 365 general protections application alleging dismissal in contravention of Part 3-1 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). The application was filed out of time after an earlier unfair dismissal application was discontinued, and the Commission refused an extension of time and dismissed the application.

Key holding: An extension of time under s 366 requires the Commission to be satisfied that exceptional circumstances exist, assessed against the s 366(2) considerations.

The Commission can extend time only if it is satisfied that there are exceptional circumstances. On balance, the considerations above do not weigh in favour of exceptional circumstances in support of an extension of time.

entry.title: United Firefighters' Union of Australia (259V) v Triple Zero Victoria [2026] FWC 4199
entry.content:
The UFU applied under s.739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for the Commission to determine whether a TZV employee was entitled to an independent investigator for serious misconduct allegations. The Commission held that neither the Triple Zero Victoria Operations Enterprise Agreement 2024 nor the TZV Workplace Investigations Procedure created that entitlement. It nonetheless recommended that Mr Walker proceed as TZV’s appointed investigator.

Key holding: Clause 67.4 requires any summary dismissal to be carried out in accordance with TZV policies and procedures consistent with the FW Act and Regulations, but it does not incorporate those policies into the Agreement or create a pre-dismissal entitlement to an independent investigation.

Properly construed, in my view, what the clause commits the Respondent to do is to enact the "summary dismissal of any employee" in accordance with its policies and procedures which must be consistent with the provisions of the Act and FW Regulations.

entry.title: CFMEU (105N) v Flinders Adelaide Container Terminal Pty Ltd Trading AS Flinders Adelaide Container Terminal [2026] FWC 4200
entry.content:
The FWC determined a dispute under the Flinders Adelaide Container Terminal Stevedoring Enterprise Agreement 2021–2025 about whether Mr Conway was entitled to permanent reclassification from Grade 3 to Grade 5. It held the 70% higher-duty threshold is a gateway only, not a mandatory entitlement, and that FACT’s refusal was consistent with the Agreement because it applied permissible merit/conduct considerations under cl 26.5.4.

Key holding: Meeting the 70% higher-duty threshold under cl 26.5.3 only permits an application and does not entitle an employee to permanent reclassification; once the gateway is met, the employer may refuse on merit principles relating to the employee’s performance, attendance, conduct or attitude.

once an employee meets the threshold of having worked seventy per cent of shifts for which they are available at a higher grade over the previous twelve months they can apply for a permanent r eclassification. Once the employee submits their application in accordance with the provisions of clause 26.5.1 and 26.5.2, the Respondent can apply merit principles as they relate to the performance or conduct of the employee to determine if the reclassification will be granted.

entry.title: Prabhatkumar Valabhai Zala v Shred-X Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4204
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission dismissed Mr Zala’s s.394 unfair dismissal application after Shred-X objected that he was not dismissed. Mr Zala resigned after a manager’s inappropriate comment and a period of psychological injury, but the Commission found Shred-X did not force him to resign. The application was dismissed for want of jurisdiction under s.386 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth).

Key holding: Whether a resignation was forced is assessed objectively by reference to the employer’s conduct, not the employee’s subjective feeling.

It is the conduct of the employer that must be assessed, not whether the employee subjectively felt like they were forced to resign.

entry.title: Claire Lin v Compass Group Remote Hospitality Services Pty Ltd & Anne Richardson and Another [2026] FWC 4201
entry.content:
Ms Lin applied under s 365 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), alleging she was dismissed after receiving an email about her fixed-term contract ending. The employer objected that she remained employed and had not been dismissed. The Commission upheld the jurisdictional objection and dismissed the application.

Key holding: A mistaken communication about a fixed-term contract ending does not amount to dismissal under s 386 where the employer has not terminated the employment relationship and the employee remains employed.

Noting that I am not satisfied that there was a termination of the contract of employment on 8 May 2026, further, I am not satisfied that there was a termination of the employment relationship. Ms Lin remained employed by the Respondent, and I am satisfied that she remains employed.

entry.title: Ms Yan Qi v Simba Education Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4193
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission considered an out-of-time unfair dismissal application by Ms Yan Qi against Simba Education Pty Ltd, filed five days after the 21-day statutory period. The Commission declined to extend time because it was not satisfied that exceptional circumstances existed. The unfair dismissal application was therefore dismissed.

Key holding: A conscious choice to contest a dismissal through alternative avenues and await the completion of those processes before filing an unfair dismissal application does not, of itself, amount to exceptional circumstances under s 394(3).

Taking into account the reason for the delay, namely a conscious choice to contest dismissal through alternative avenues and waiting for those processes to be complete before making the unfair dismissal application, does not amount to exceptional circumstances .

entry.title: Mr Steven Kelly v P.G. Higham Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4206
entry.content:
This was a s.365 general protections application in which Mr Kelly alleged dismissal after presenting for work following a workers’ compensation injury. The employer denied dismissal and said he remained on its books as a casual. The Commission upheld the jurisdictional objection and dismissed the application because Mr Kelly was not dismissed.

Key holding: A refusal to permit an employee to attend work is not a dismissal under s.386 where the employee lacks medical clearance and the employer remains willing to offer work once fitness is certified.

I am not satisfied that there was a termination of the contract of employment on 22 June 2026, nor am I satisfied that there was a termination of the employment relationship. The Respondent has been prepared to consider Mr Kelly's fitness for work and offer work when he was certified fit for pre-injury duties.

entry.title: Emily Lowe v Home n Heaven Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4176
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission considered a jurisdictional objection to an unfair dismissal application by Ms Lowe against Home n Heaven Pty Ltd. The employer argued Ms Lowe had not served the minimum employment period because she had only 189 days’ service after a business purchase. The Commission found a transfer of employment occurred, so her prior service counted as continuous service.

Key holding: A probationary term in a new employment contract cannot override the statutory continuity of service arising from a transfer of employment under the Fair Work Act 2009.

The fact that the company purported to offer probationary employment to Ms Lowe does not override the provisions of the Act.

entry.title: Application by Birrang Enterprise Development Co Ltd [2026] FWC 4167
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission considered Birrang’s application under s 120 of the Fair Work Act 2009 to reduce Mr Reid’s redundancy pay because it had offered him redeployment into a Support Coordinator role. Mr Reid declined the role but consented to the application. The Commission reduced his redundancy entitlement from four weeks to three weeks’ pay.

Key holding: Under s 120(1)(b)(i), whether alternative employment is acceptable is assessed objectively by the Commission, not by the employee’s subjective view, and if the preconditions are met the Commission has a broad discretion under s 120(2) to reduce redundancy pay.

Whether the alternative employment is "acceptable" is to be determined objectively, not by reference to whether Mr Reid considered that it was subjectively acceptable. The determination of whether alternative employment is acceptable requires me to make an assessment and value judgment.

She filed 82 days out of time and sought an extension under s 366(1) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). The Fair Work Commission refused the extension and dismissed the application.

entry.title: Estefania Asensio Tato v Lycée Condorcet Trading AS The International French School Of Sydney Ltd [2026] FWC 4154
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission dealt with a s 739 dispute brought by a former secondary Spanish teacher against her former school over alleged underpayments/classification for February and March 2025 work. The Commission upheld the school’s jurisdictional objection because the dispute was not raised until after employment ended, dismissed the application, and noted any underpayment claim could be pursued in court. The deed of release was not determinative.

Key holding: Under s 739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), the Commission lacks jurisdiction to determine an enterprise agreement dispute where the dispute is raised after the employment relationship has ended.

The entitlements conferred in the Agreement remain enforceable for a limited period on application to the relevant Court, but the Commission is unable to deal with the dispute under the dispute resolution clause where the dispute was raised after the employment relationship had ended.

entry.title: Ms Joy Bultman v The Trustee For Scrappy's Metal Recycling Trust [2026] FWC 4149
entry.content:
Ms Joy Bultman applied under s.394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for an unfair dismissal remedy against The Trustee For Scrappy’s Metal Recycling Trust. She failed to attend a Commission mention/conference, did not comply with directions, filed no material by the deadline, and gave no explanation. Deputy President Bell dismissed the application for want of prosecution and no reasonable prospects of success in Bultman v The Trustee For Scrappy’s Metal Recycling Trust [2026] FWC 4149.

Key holding: Under s.587(1) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), the Commission may dismiss an application for failure to prosecute, including non-compliance with directions or failure to attend, and where no evidence means no reasonable prospects of success.

I am satisfied the power to dismiss can extend to circumstances where an applicant has failed to prosecute his or her case, including by non -compliance with directions to attend a mention/conference or file material and a repeated failure to provide a proper explanation for that non -compliance.

entry.title: Application by dnata Airport Services Pty Ltd Trading AS dnata [2026] FWC 4178
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission considered whether to approve dnata’s Queensland passenger services enterprise agreement [2026] FWC 4178. The TWU opposed approval, arguing the Agreement did not pass the better off overall test (BOOT), particularly regarding part-time shiftworker overtime and pay rates that might fall below the Award. The Commission largely accepted dnata’s Award construction and BOOT approach, but required further information or an undertaking about part-time day workers before approval.

Key holding: The BOOT is assessed at the test time, and the Commission does not speculate about future unknown Award wage outcomes when deciding whether employees are better off overall.

I accept the Applicant 's submission to the effect that it is not for the Commission to speculate about potential future unknown wage outcomes in assessing the BOOT, and that the BOOT is to be applied at test time.

entry.title: Ms Karen McClear v A Team Tuition Australia Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4174
entry.content:
Ms McClear resigned after a lengthy suspension pending an unresolved misconduct investigation and brought a s 365 general protections claim alleging she was forced to resign. A Team Tuition objected that she was not dismissed within s 386. The Commission dismissed the application, finding she was not forced to resign because of the employer’s conduct and was therefore not dismissed.

Key holding: A resignation is a dismissal under s 386(1)(b) only where an objective assessment of the employer’s conduct shows it made resignation the probable result or left the employee with no effective or real choice but to resign.

In making that assessment, it is appropriate to make an objective analysis of the Respondent's conduct to determine whether it was of such a nature that resignation was the probable result or that the employee had no effective or real choice but to resign.

entry.title: Ms Mariama Serray Turay v Pegasus Community Care Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4186
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission dealt with Ms Turay’s unfair dismissal application, which was filed before the dismissal ultimately relied on took effect. The Commission found her employment was terminated on 16 September 2026 after an earlier 30 June 2026 termination notice was withdrawn by consent, so the 7 September 2026 application was premature. The Commission declined to waive the irregularity and dismissed the application.

Key holding: The Commission may decline to waive the irregularity in a premature unfair dismissal application where the applicant had a clear opportunity to withdraw and file a new application within time but did not do so.

As to whether Ms Turay could have discontinued the Application and filed a new application within time, this factor weights against waiving the irregularity.

entry.title: "Automotive, Food, Metals, Engineering, Printing and Kindred Industries Union" known as the Australian Manufacturing Workers' Union (AMWU) (188V) v Applus Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4190
entry.content:
The AMWU applied under s 739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for the Fair Work Commission to resolve a dispute over clause 17.2 of the Applus Pty Ltd Onshore NDT & Inspection Greenfields Agreement 2025. The issue was whether Easter Saturday and Easter Sunday, both falling on a weekend, entitled employees to public holidays on the next two working days or only the next working day. The Commission held each public holiday had to be taken on successive next working days.

Key holding: Under clause 17.2, where two gazetted public holidays fall on a weekend, each holiday must be taken on successive next working days so employees receive both entitlements.

Having considered the text, context and purpose, I find that the answer to the question is that employees were entitled to take the Easter Saturday public holiday on Tuesday, 7 April 2026, and the Easter Sunday public holiday on Wednesday, 8 April 2026.

entry.title: "Automotive, Food, Metals, Engineering, Printing and Kindred Industries Union" known as the Australian Manufacturing Workers' Union (AMWU) (188V) v Schindler Lifts Australia Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4166
entry.content:
The AMWU referred a dispute under s.739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) and clause 10 of the Schindler Lifts Australia Pty Ltd Victorian Enterprise Agreement 2024–2028, asking how the "make up pay for workers comp" entitlement in clause 42 is calculated. The Commission held that "average weekly earnings" in clause 42 is to be worked out by reference to the Victorian workers' compensation concept of pre-injury average weekly earnings under the WIRC Act, and left the arithmetic to the parties.

Key holding: Where an enterprise agreement requires a top-up to 100% of "average weekly earnings" but does not define the term, that expression is to be calculated by reference to the pre-injury average weekly earnings concept in the Victorian workers' compensation legislation, with either s.153(1) or s.153(2) of the WIRC Act available.

As such, I consider that Mr Savari's 'average weekly earnings' for the purposes of clause 42 of the 2024 Agreement in relation to his workers' compensation claim for injury for the injury on 20 March 2025 are able to be calculated by reference to either s.153(1) or s.153(2) of the WIRC Act.

entry.title: Madana Harrop v Maryborough District Health Service [2026] FWC 4112
entry.content:
Ms Harrop lodged an unfair dismissal application 16 days late after her union, the ANMF, failed to transmit a legal referral due to an automated email system error. The Fair Work Commission accepted representative error as a reasonable explanation, found exceptional circumstances and granted an extension of time. The merits of the unfair dismissal claim have not yet been determined.

The Commission found he had not been acting at the higher classification level in the same role for a continuous two-year period, so the decision was not a 'conversion decision' and was not appealable under s 132(1)(k) of the Public Sector Act 2022 (Qld). The appeal was not heard for want of jurisdiction.

entry.content:
The applicant commenced proceedings in the Queensland Industrial Relations Commission alleging she was dismissed for a prohibited reason after raising work health and safety concerns. The respondent sought dismissal on the basis that the applicant had already litigated the same material facts in the Federal Circuit and Family Court under the Fair Work Act.
